document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: These joint EANO and ESMO recommendations address diagnosis, prevention, treatment and follow-up of parenchymal brain metastasis (BM) arising from solid tumours. They complement the societies’ earlier guidance on leptomeningeal metastasis. BM originating from primary brain tumours, lymphoma or leukaemia is outside their scope, as are differential diagnosis, adverse effects of treatment and comprehensive supportive or palliative care. Because evidence is often limited, many recommendations rely on expert judgement and consensus rather than informative clinical trials. The intended readers include clinicians, other health care providers, informed patients and relatives.

document_sections.heading: INCIDENCE AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
document_sections.content: Further information about epidemiology and pathogenesis is provided in the supplementary material.

document_sections.heading: DIAGNOSIS, PATHOLOGY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY Clinical presentation
document_sections.content: Neurological manifestations commonly develop over weeks. BM may produce headache, seizures, hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, personality change, aphasia, visual disturbance or manifestations of increased intracranial pressure. Seizure risk probably relates to cortical proximity and tumour haemorrhage; focal findings vary with lesion location. Haemorrhage, particularly in metastases from melanoma or chorionic carcinoma, and obstructive hydrocephalus, particularly with cerebellar BM, can precipitate rapid deterioration. A detailed neurological examination using a standard form, such as that proposed by RANO, should be recorded at diagnosis and throughout follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic procedures
document_sections.content: New neurological findings in a patient with cancer warrant neurological assessment and imaging to distinguish BM from other causes, including treatment effects. Screening when the primary cancer is diagnosed is probably warranted for lung cancer, particularly non-squamous disease, with a possible exception for stage I NSCLC. It should also be considered for stage IV melanoma because earlier detection may affect decisions and outcomes, and may be justified for metastatic HER2-positive or triple-negative breast cancer [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Screening increases detection of asymptomatic BM. Approximately 75% of BM occur in cerebral hemispheres, 21% in the cerebellum and up to 3% in the brain stem. Fewer than half are single brain lesions; very few are solitary metastases in the body. Cranial MRI before and after contrast, using at least 1.5-T, is the reference neuroradiological examination. Suspected BM requires, at minimum, pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted and/or T2-FLAIR, and DWI sequences [EANO III, C; ESMO IV, B]. Typical features are solid or ring enhancement, surrounding oedema and occurrence at the grey–white junction or vascular border zones. MRS, perfusion imaging and DWI may add findings such as tumour-associated metabolites, unrestricted diffusion in cystic contents and low perfusion, but no imaging-feature combination identifies BM with complete certainty. Consider biopsy when a lesion, especially a cystic one, cannot confidently be differentiated from a primary brain tumour, abscess or inflammatory lesion. MRI sensitivity varies with field strength, contrast agent and dose, post-contrast delay and spatial resolution. Three-dimensional acquisition is preferred for its thinner sections. Double-dose contrast improves sensitivity but reduces specificity and should be reserved for circumstances in which maximising sensitivity is essential. Allow at least several minutes between contrast administration and post-contrast T1-weighted acquisition, for example by acquiring another sequence in between. Cranial CT is substantially less sensitive and should be restricted to patients who cannot undergo MRI. Extracranial FDGePET detects more extracranial metastases than CT and improves staging accuracy, particularly when the primary cancer is unknown; normal cerebral FDG uptake, however, markedly limits its sensitivity for BM. Radiolabelled amino acid PET adds diagnostic information to anatomical MRI and performs better than FDGePET in patients with brain tumours, including BM.

document_sections.heading: Pathology and liquid biopsies
document_sections.content: The supplementary material contains further pathology and liquid-biopsy information. An identification algorithm establishes the likely tissue of origin for most BM. Table 1 provides predictive markers by tumour entity; their value for directing treatment varies with disease location and extent and with subsequent identification of the primary, so the table is orientative. Figure 1 presents typical immunohistochemical profiles for investigating metastatic carcinoma of unknown primary. These profiles often help identify origin, but exceptions occur, particularly in less differentiated cancers. Squamous cell and neuroendocrine carcinoma metastases can be especially difficult to assign to a tissue of origin because informative immunohistochemical markers may be absent. DNA methylation, RNA and miRNA platforms have potential for identifying the origin of cancers of unknown primary but are not yet routine clinical methods.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Consider screening for BM in lung cancer, possibly excluding stage I NSCLC, and in stage IV melanoma; screening may also be appropriate in metastatic HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Investigate BM by neuroimaging in any patient with cancer who develops signs or symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, seizures or new neurological deficits [EANO III, B; ESMO III, B]. For suspected BM, obtain cranial MRI with pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted and/or T2-FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted sequences [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Use local institutional algorithms for histopathological and immunohistochemical assessment [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. After neurosurgical resection, confirm in the BM any treatment-relevant predictive biomarkers previously identified in the primary tumour or metastases outside the CNS [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Do not routinely order blood or CSF cell-free tumour DNA testing to characterise or monitor BM [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, C]. If clinical or imaging findings raise suspicion of leptomeningeal metastasis, perform CSF investigations, including cytology, to exclude it [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, B].

document_sections.heading: THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES: GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
document_sections.content: For most patients, BM treatment aims to avert or postpone neurological decline and extend survival while preserving acceptable quality of life. A minority, especially those with few small lesions, may survive long term or be cured. Treatment commonly combines several tumour-directed approaches.

document_sections.heading: Surgery
document_sections.content: Diagnostic neurosurgery is needed in several circumstances: uncertain imaging diagnosis, unknown primary, more than one known tumour, a primary tumour that rarely metastasises to the brain, or potentially decision-changing differences in molecular profile between BM and the primary [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, B]. After SRT, biopsy has limited capacity to distinguish progression from treatment effects because viable tumour and changes such as necrosis may coexist and may not both appear in the sample. The therapeutic benefit of resecting at least a single BM in a patient with controlled systemic disease is well established. Resection extent is associated with local control [EANO: I, A; ESMO: II, A]. En bloc rather than piecemeal excision may reduce recurrence and leptomeningeal spread. Preoperative functional MRI, intraoperative neuronavigation, fluorescence guidance and cortical mapping can improve the prospect of gross total resection with low morbidity. Obtain postoperative MRI within 48 h to assess resection extent. Historical randomised trials found better survival with resection followed by WBRT than with WBRT alone for single BM, but were conducted with older imaging and surgical techniques, without active systemic treatments, and commonly combined different primary cancers. Extrapolation to current practice has prompted the assumption—not trial confirmation—that gross total resection of more than one BM might yield comparable improvement. In multiple BM, consider surgery for an immediate effect when a large lesion (>3 cm diameter) causes increased intracranial pressure or neurological impairment in an eloquent area. Posterior fossa lesions often warrant surgery because of obstructive-hydrocephalus risk. Cystic or necrotic lesions may respond less well to SRT; aspiration followed by radiosurgery is another possible approach. Resection permits faster steroid reduction than other interventions and may improve subsequent treatment, particularly immune checkpoint inhibition. Surgery is less commonly indicated for recurrent BM, although individual circumstances, including promising further systemic treatment, can support it. Laser interstitial thermal therapy has encouraging local-control data in recurrent brain tumours and radiation necrosis, but its BM role needs further study. Apart from emergencies, a multidisciplinary tumour board should weigh surgical risks and benefits, including surgery versus SRT and the tissue quantity and quality needed for molecular neuropathology. This is particularly important because most patients with BM die from systemic disease rather than BM.

document_sections.heading: Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: WBRT was historically the principal radiation treatment for BM, whereas SRS is now standard care in many settings. The subsequent subsections describe stereotactic treatment, WBRT and prophylactic cranial irradiation.

document_sections.heading: Stereotactic radiosurgery
document_sections.content: SRS delivers high-dose radiation to an intracranial target using stereotactic or image guidance with approximately 1 mm targeting accuracy. Single-fraction treatment commonly uses 15 to 24 Gy. Fractionated SRS uses two to five fractions, typically 27 Gy in three fractions or 30 Gy in five fractions, and is preferred for lesions >3 cm diameter, lesions near vulnerable structures such as the brain stem, or previously irradiated patients. Adding SRS to WBRT improves OS for 1-3 BM. SRS is increasingly used for >3 BM. In the prospective multicentre JLGK0901 study, 1194 patients with 1-10 BM received SRS alone; survival was similar at 10.8 months for the 2-4 and 5-10 BM groups. Treatment toxicity was low, and mini-mental state examination results were similar between groups when total tumour volume was <15 ml. Because recurrence after surgery alone is frequent, two randomised trials assessed cavity SRS. Brown et al. assigned 194 patients to postoperative WBRT or SRS: OS did not differ, while cognitive decline occurred more frequently with WBRT. Mahajan et al. assigned 132 patients to postoperative SRS or observation and found significantly greater freedom from local recurrence with SRS. For larger cavities, risk-adapted dosing across three to five fractions is encouraged.

document_sections.heading: Whole-brain radiotherapy
document_sections.content: WBRT, usually 20-30 Gy in 5-10 fractions, has been used after local therapy or as initial treatment, chiefly for multiple BM. Following surgery or SRS for limited BM, it improved intracranial local and distant control but not OS, and worsened neurocognitive function. A randomised phase III trial likewise demonstrated no benefit from WBRT after local treatment of one to three melanoma BM. Initial WBRT for multiple BM is associated with median survival of 3-6 months and 10%-15% survival at 1 year. QUARTZ randomised patients with NSCLC ineligible for surgery or SRT between optimal supportive care and the same care plus WBRT (20 Gy in five fractions). Both groups had similar median survival of approximately 9 weeks; supportive care alone did not produce a significant quality-of-life reduction. WBRT may nevertheless have a place for multiple large unresectable lesions in newly diagnosed cancer, younger patients or those with good PS. A simultaneous integrated boost increases the focal dose to visible lesions relative to WBRT alone. RTOG 0614 suggested a trend towards cognitive protection with memantine plus WBRT. NRG CC001 compared WBRT plus memantine against HA-WBRT plus memantine and found significantly better preservation of patient-reported quality of life and prevention of cognitive decline across follow-up in the HA-WBRT group. The contribution of memantine remains uncertain: memantine with conventional WBRT was not active, and its role in the activity of HA-WBRT cannot be established.

document_sections.heading: Prophylactic cranial irradiation
document_sections.content: PCI is established standard care for limited and extensive SCLC. In extensive-stage disease, toxicity concerns and the introduction of serial MRI surveillance and immune checkpoint inhibition challenge its use. A randomised phase III trial found that adding hippocampal avoidance to PCI did not reduce the likelihood of cognitive decline relative to standard PCI; BM incidence at 2 years and survival also did not differ. Hippocampal sparing therefore cannot be regarded as standard care in this setting.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: Most BM enhance on MRI or CT, indicating absence of a functional blood–brain barrier in those lesions. The distribution of intravenous drugs might therefore resemble that of intravenous imaging contrast, potentially allowing systemic therapy to work as effectively in enhancing BM as in extracranial disease. Whether gadolinium uptake predicts adequate entry of larger molecules, including monoclonal antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates, is uncertain. Drug selection depends primarily on tumour histology and molecular features rather than intracranial location. When feasible, consider molecular genetic analysis of BM instead of the primary to select tumour-specific targeted therapy or immunotherapy [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Better blood–brain barrier penetration is predicted to improve control, especially where that barrier remains partially intact. Decisions should account for prior treatment and, where several systemic options exist, CNS and extracranial activity and each option’s toxicity [EANO: IV, A; ESMO: IV, B]. Preliminary evidence suggests steroid exposure adversely affects immunotherapy outcomes in BM.

document_sections.heading: BM from breast cancer
document_sections.content: Systemic treatment contributes substantially to BM control. Agents used include capecitabine, cyclophosphamide, 5-fluorouracil, methotrexate, vincristine, cisplatin, etoposide, vinorelbine and gemcitabine; most have response rates >30%. Targeted therapy is particularly relevant to HER2-positive metastatic disease. Among patients without a surgical indication, with PS 0-2, previously given trastuzumab but not capecitabine–lapatinib, lapatinib plus capecitabine yielded brain responses of 38% in previously irradiated BM and 66% in treatment-naïve BM. In the second/third-line NALA study comparing neratinib plus capecitabine with lapatinib plus capecitabine, 130 participants entered with stable, asymptomatic BM; the ‘overall cumulative incidence’ of BM intervention, mostly RT, fell from 29% to 23% in the neratinib arm (P = 0.04). A phase II study of neratinib plus capecitabine found a control rate approaching 50% (22 partial response, 16 stable disease) among patients previously treated with surgery and/or RT, receiving a stable steroid dose and predominantly treated with more than two systemic lines. In a secondary EMILIA analysis of patients previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane and retrospectively identified as having asymptomatic CNS metastases (n = 95), median OS was 26.8 months with T-DM1 (n = 45) versus 12.9 months with lapatinib plus capecitabine (n = 50). A retrospective T-DM1 analysis, in which 92% had undergone local therapy, reported a response rate up to 44%. In third-line HER2CLIMB, half the participants had BM. Among the 291 participants with BM, median OS was significantly longer with tucatinib, capecitabine and trastuzumab than with trastuzumab and capecitabine (18.1 versus 12.0 months). Few studies specifically address systemic therapy for HER2-negative luminal or triple-negative BM. In heavily pretreated estrogen receptor-positive/HER2-negative BM, abemaciclib produced an intracranial clinical benefit rate of 25%, defined by complete or partial response or stable disease lasting 6 months, and median PFS of 4.4 months. Systemic prevention of BM is an emerging issue. In CLEOPATRA, participants had no BM at diagnosis, but 13% had brain relapse at first recurrence; within that subgroup, adding pertuzumab to trastuzumab and docetaxel increased median time to BM from 12 to 15 months. CEREBEL did not show superior first- or second-line BM prevention with lapatinib plus capecitabine versus trastuzumab plus capecitabine.

document_sections.heading: BM from lung cancer
document_sections.content: For advanced NSCLC without an actionable driver, standard care includes anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 monotherapy when PD-L1 is positive (>50%), or immune checkpoint inhibition combined with platinum-based chemotherapy. Additional combinations involving CTLA-4 inhibition, with or without chemotherapy, have entered practice. Evidence specific to asymptomatic BM remains scarce: early pembrolizumab data suggested safety and CNS response rates around 30% in untreated NSCLC BM; retrospective data supported nivolumab activity in asymptomatic BM. Combination-trial subgroup analyses suggest significant intracranial activity with anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA4, with or without chemotherapy, and similar benefit regardless of CNS involvement. Most immunotherapy trials included only controlled, previously treated BM, often after RT, and limited prospective evidence constrains conclusions for untreated asymptomatic BM. A pooled multicentre analysis reported a 27.3% intracranial response rate among patients designated as having ‘active’ BM (n = 73). NSCLC with EGFR mutation or ALK, ROS1 or RET rearrangement has a higher cumulative BM incidence than NSCLC lacking driver oncogenes. Reported median survival is >3 years with EGFR-mutated NSCLC and >5 years with ALK rearrangement. TKIs are a standard element of multimodal care because intracranial and extracranial response rates exceed those with conventional chemotherapy. Intracranial response varies with drug potency, blood–brain barrier penetration and P-glycoprotein interactions. CNS activity has been shown for specific TKIs in tumours with EGFR mutations, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK or NRG1 rearrangements, or MET exon 14 skipping mutations. Evidence on targeted treatment of KRAS G12C and BRAF mutations is limited. For extensive SCLC, standard care combines platinum, etoposide and immune checkpoint inhibition [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. Its additional value specifically in SCLC with BM remains to be formally established, irrespective of symptoms or local treatment.

document_sections.heading: BM from melanoma
document_sections.content: Conventional temozolomide, dacarbazine and fotemustine have limited activity against melanoma BM. In BRAF-mutated disease, vemurafenib or dabrafenib monotherapy yielded intracranial responses between 15% and 40%. The reported combination of vemurafenib and dabrafenib achieved responses up to 60% in untreated asymptomatic BM, comparable to other organs, but responses were generally short. Anti-PD-1 monotherapy and ipilimumab plus nivolumab have been studied in BM. For asymptomatic patients, available data favour the combination, with an overall response rate of approximately 50%, reasonable response duration and PFS of >50% at 18 months. Trial eligibility was stringent, producing asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic populations with low CNS tumour burden. Accordingly, ipilimumab plus nivolumab is the preferred first-line approach even for asymptomatic BRAF-mutated BM [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. Its apparent intracranial response is lower, at 21%, in symptomatic patients requiring steroids.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations Surgery
document_sections.content: Consider surgery for an uncertain neoplastic diagnosis, unknown primary, more than one known tumour, a primary that rarely causes BM, or potentially decision-changing molecular differences from the primary [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Consider resection for a single BM [EANO: I, A; ESMO: II, A]. Resection may be considered for multiple resectable BM [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: V, C], and for patients receiving steroids who are candidates for immune checkpoint inhibition [EANO: III, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Consider surgery for acute manifestations of raised intracranial pressure [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Obtain MRI within 48 h postoperatively to establish resection extent [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: V, C].

document_sections.heading: Radiotherapy SRS is recommended for patients with a limited number (1-4) of BMs [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A]. SRS may be considered for patients with a higher number of BMs (5-10) with a cumulative tumour volume <15 ml [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. SRS to the resection cavity is recommended after complete or incomplete resection of BMs [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A].
document_sections.content: Recommend SRS for 1-4 BM [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A]. SRS may be considered for 5-10 BM if cumulative tumour volume is <15 ml [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. Recommend cavity SRS after either complete or incomplete BM resection [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A]. Discourage postoperative WBRT after resection or SRS [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, E]. Consider WBRT for multiple BM unsuitable for SRS according to symptoms, lesion size, number and location, and available CNS-active systemic options [EANO: III, B; ESMO: III, B]. For multiple BM unsuitable for SRS with poor PS, consider supportive care without WBRT [EANO: I, B; ESMO: I, B]. Despite reservations, PCI remains recommended after complete response to chemoradiotherapy in limited or extensive-stage SCLC [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A].

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy Systemic pharmacotherapy based on histological and molecular characteristics of the primary tumour and previous treatment should be considered for most patients with BMs [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B].
document_sections.content: Consider systemic pharmacotherapy for most patients, guided by primary-tumour histology, molecular characteristics and previous therapy [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. If feasible, consider analysing BM rather than primary-tumour genetics when choosing tumour-specific targeted therapy or immunotherapy [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: IV, B]. In HER2-positive breast cancer with preserved general status and asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic BM, consider systemic therapy to defer WBRT [EANO: III, C; ESMO: III; B]. After local therapy, progressive HER2-negative breast cancer BM may be treated with standard chemotherapy such as capecitabine, eribulin or carboplatin and bevacizumab [EANO: III, C; ESMO: III, B]. For asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic NSCLC BM without an actionable driver, give upfront immune checkpoint inhibition alone at PD-L1 50%, or chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibition at PD-L1 <50% [EANO: II, B; ESMO: III, B]. For similarly symptomatic NSCLC BM with an actionable alteration such as EGFR or ALK or ROS1 rearrangement, give upfront systemic targeted therapy [EANO: II, B; ESMO: III, B]. Treat SCLC with platinum-based chemotherapy, with or without immune checkpoint inhibition [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. Prefer first-line ipilimumab plus nivolumab in asymptomatic patients with either BRAF wild-type or BRAF-mutated melanoma [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, B]. Eligible patients with multiple symptomatic BRAF-mutated BM or requiring 4 mg dexamethasone or more should receive dabrafenib plus trametinib [EANO: IV, B; ESMO: IV, B].

document_sections.heading: INTEGRATED THERAPEUTIC APPROACHES
document_sections.content: Choose combined approaches according to general and neurological condition, comorbidity, imaging, primary-tumour histology and preferably updated molecular status, and prior therapy. Estimate individually the contributions of surgery, radiation and medical oncology; ideally, discuss decisions in a dedicated BM or disease-specific tumour board with CNS expertise [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Surgery and SRT can compete or complement each other for local control. WBRT use is declining because its benefit–risk balance is modest and SRS has developed. An unknown primary, uncertain imaging diagnosis, large cystic or necrotic lesion, high-dose steroid requirement, mass effect or need for decision-guiding molecular profiling favours resection. Difficult surgical access, elevated operative risk or preference for non-invasive outpatient treatment favours SRS alone over surgery commonly followed by SRS or systemic therapy. Systemic treatment should principally reflect primary-tumour histology, molecular features and previous therapy. For BM-CUP despite extensive work-up, notably PET, controlled-trial data are unavailable. Resection should be followed by cavity RT; without other tumour manifestations, tumour-agnostic systemic therapy should not follow unless an actionable driver mutation is found. Assess toxicity when combining each new systemic drug with RT: BRAF inhibitors with WBRT can cause severe dermatitis, usually addressed by avoiding concurrent delivery. No prospective trial has established optimal combinations of systemic therapy, including TKI or checkpoint inhibition, and surgery or SRS for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic BM; such trials need survival, quality-of-life and neurocognitive outcomes. In breast cancer, the optimal timing of systemic therapy relative to RT is undetermined, and most trials examine systemic drugs alone. For NSCLC without activating drivers and with limited asymptomatic BM, a systematic meta-analysis largely based on uncontrolled evidence suggests better OS with early checkpoint inhibition plus SRS than with sequential treatment. Retrospective EGFR-mutated NSCLC studies, mostly using first-generation inhibitors with poor CNS penetration, likewise suggest the best survival with upfront TKI plus SRT rather than sequencing. Controlled trials must establish whether potent brain-penetrant agents, including osimertinib, remove the need for early SRS. Evidence on TKI–local therapy sequencing with ALK translocation is even more limited, although consensus opposes upfront WBRT for EGFR-mutated or ALK-translocated disease. In SCLC BM, symptoms and disease burden determine whether and when to add SRS or WBRT. Replacing WBRT with SRS appears to worsen time to CNS progression without changing OS. Despite melanoma’s radioresistance, SRS can provide durable local control. Its optimal place in melanoma multimodal treatment remains unsettled, although uncontrolled cohorts support early combinations. Randomised evidence confirming superiority of initial combined modalities has not been published; whether selection bias explains cohort findings is disputed. Systemic therapy is also considered for symptomatic BM, usually not alone. After imaging or tissue confirmation of progression, ideally review options at a multidisciplinary board; depending on the individual case, consider surgery, repeat SRS, systemic-treatment change or combinations. Randomised BM trials are needed to establish intervention timing, including surgery before immunotherapy and SRS at diagnosis alongside systemic therapy versus at progression. Consider clinical-trial enrolment whenever possible.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Base multimodal BM management on an individual assessment of surgery, radiation oncology and medical oncology contributions [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Ideally discuss treatment in a dedicated BM board or disease-specific board involving CNS-tumour expertise [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Conduct randomised trials in asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic BM to identify optimal combinations of surgery or SRS with systemic treatment, including TKI or immune checkpoint inhibition [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B].

document_sections.heading: MONITORING AND FOLLOW-UP
document_sections.content: Follow patients with prior BM through neurological assessment and imaging at 3-monthly intervals and whenever clinically indicated. Figure 2 outlines proposed multimodal pathways for BM generally, SCLC and melanoma: uncertain diagnosis or unknown primary prompts biopsy or resection followed by early (≤48 h) postoperative MRI or CT as a monitoring baseline. It separates favourable factors—1-10 BM depending on total volume, controlled extracranial disease, preserved performance status and expected survival >3 months—from unfavourable factors including >10 BM, uncontrolled extracranial disease and expected survival <3 months. Options shown include surgery followed by SRS/SRT, SRS/SRT alone, systemic treatment, WBRT in specified circumstances and palliative care; at progression, prior treatment and clinical condition guide further choices. The SCLC pathway conditions WBRT options on absence of previous PCI or WBRT. RANO response criteria, increasingly used in trials and practice, incorporate contrast-enhanced MRI changes in target and non-target lesions, neurological status and steroid use. Record neurological function regularly using a standardised method, such as the neurologic assessment in neuro-oncology scale. Assess cognition initially and during the illness, and repeatedly reassess capacity to consent [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Obtain brain MRI every 2-3 months or whenever neurological progression is suspected [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. MRI is the standard follow-up and response-assessment method; repeat it on the same scanner or one with identical field strength. Conventional MRI may not reliably separate pseudoprogression or radionecrosis from tumour progression. Perfusion MRI and MRS are increasingly employed, but evidence that they improve this distinction is limited. Following RT, studies of amino acid PET tracers [11C]-methyl-L-methionine, 3,4-dihydroxy-6-[18F]-fluoro-L-phenylalanine and FET report both sensitivity and specificity in the range of 80%-90% for differentiating recurrence from radiation injury. FET PET may also help identify treatment-related changes after checkpoint inhibition or targeted treatment, with or without RT [EANO III, C; ESMO IV, C]. Immunotherapy RANO criteria allow for delayed responses so that initial progression is not prematurely classified as treatment failure; prolonged survival and regression can follow early apparent progression. Pseudoprogression appears uncommon with immunotherapy alone. More research is needed to differentiate treatment change from progression after SRT, with or without systemic therapy. If the primary remains unidentified after the initial work-up, whole-body FDGePET during follow-up may help. Circulating tumour-cell and cell-free DNA assays in blood or CSF are not yet part of BM response assessment or follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Perform a detailed neurological examination every 2-3 months, or sooner if imaging suggests progression or neurological findings appear [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, B]. Reassess cognition and capacity to consent regularly [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Obtain brain MRI every 2-3 months and whenever neurological progression is suspected [EANO: IV, C; ESMO: IV, B]. Consider advanced MRI, including MRS and perfusion imaging, and amino acid PET to distinguish treatment effects from tumour progression [EANO: III, C; ESMO: IV, C].

document_sections.heading: SUPPORTIVE CARE
document_sections.content: This guideline does not comprehensively cover BM palliation or supportive care; general brain-tumour principles apply. When steroids are clinically necessary for increased intracranial pressure, use the lowest dose for the shortest feasible period [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Steroid use lasting more than a few weeks increases Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia risk; consider trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis when additional immunosuppressive systemic treatment is given. Bevacizumab is probably the best treatment for radionecrosis after SRT, with activity superior to steroids, and probably does not impair immunotherapy efficacy. Following a seizure, give secondary anticonvulsant prophylaxis at least temporarily. Do not use primary anticonvulsant prophylaxis: prevention of a first seizure has not been shown [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A]. Prefer anticonvulsants without drug interactions, such as levetiracetam, lamotrigine and lacosamide, over phenytoin, carbamazepine or valproic acid. Consider primary thromboprophylaxis during hospitalisation for acute illness or confinement to bed. LMWH or unfractionated heparin is recommended for primary prophylaxis and VTE treatment [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, C]. BM-related thromboembolic risks include particular primary cancers, steroids, chemotherapy, high body mass index and immobility. Therapeutic LMWH probably does not increase intracranial bleeding risk in BM overall, although other bleeding risks must be assessed. Data on direct oral anticoagulants in BM are lacking.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Consider steroids only for symptomatic patients [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: IV, B]. Do not give primary anticonvulsant prophylaxis [EANO: I, A; ESMO: I, A]. When indicated, consider LMWH first line for primary or secondary thromboprophylaxis and treatment of VTE in BM [EANO: II, B; ESMO: II, C]. Driving-competence decisions must consider seizures, cognition and other neurological abilities and comply with national law and guidance [EANO: IV, n/a; ESMO: V, n/a].

document_sections.heading: OUTLOOK
document_sections.content: Guidance reflects evidence and consensus at a particular time, and updates will be announced on EANO and ESMO websites. Secondary analyses dividing BM into poorly defined ‘active’ and ‘inactive’ groups cannot support treatment algorithms. Improving outcomes for individual primary cancers requires dedicated BM trials with clearly defined diagnosis and entry criteria, molecular enrichment where feasible, and suitable evaluation criteria.

document_sections.heading: METHODOLOGY
document_sections.content: The guideline followed ESMO procedures for developing Clinical Practice Guidelines. Expert authors selected relevant literature, using PubMed searches combining ‘CNS’, ‘brain’, ‘metastasis’, ‘trial’, ‘clinical’, ‘surgery’, ‘radiotherapy’, ‘chemotherapy’, ‘targeted therapy’, ‘immunotherapy’, ‘imaging’, ‘MRI’ and ‘PET’ from 1 January 2011 to 30 August 2020, alongside papers from their own files. Review was limited to English-language papers. Authors agreed the final references on originality and relevance across the guideline’s scope. Evidence levels and recommendation grades use European Federation of Neurological Societies criteria recommended by EANO and an adapted Infectious Disease Society of America-United States Public Health Service Grading System recommended by ESMO. The experts regarded ungraded statements as justified standard clinical practice.
